title: Greedy Best-First in Lisbon: Fast but risky ⚡
description: Watch Greedy Best-First sprint toward the destination in a real city-style grid, using only a heuristic. Then see exactly why it can get trapped or take a detour when the “closest-looking” path is a mirage.
ig_caption:
Greedy Best-First Search vs A*: Pathfinding Comparison — Why it rushes to the goal ⚡ (and when it fails)

In Lisbon (Alfama), we run **Greedy Best-First** with a heuristic (h) that estimates “distance to goal.” Unlike A*, it **doesn’t balance cost so far (g)**—it prioritizes nodes with the smallest **h(n)**.

What you’ll see in the animation:
• It aggressively expands the option that *looks* closest to the exit.
• If obstacles force a longer route, Greedy can **turn early**, oscillate, or **get stuck** near the goal frontage.

Takeaway: Greedy Best-First can be blazing-fast when the heuristic is well-behaved, but it’s not guaranteed to find the shortest path.

Debate question: Would you rather optimize for **speed** (Greedy) or **optimality** (A*) when roadblocks appear?
